results.title: What is HIL Testing?
results.content: Model-Based Systems Engineering Requirements validation through simulation Embedded Software & Controls Architect, design, and verify embedded systems System Integration Test Center Enhance the safety of EV systems Analytics & IoT Guide for connected solutions Architecture & AUTOSAR AUTOSAR framework architecture Data Operations Edge‑to‑cloud, and smart factory enablement Rapid Prototyping Accelerate development by early-stage testing. The phrase Hardware-In-the-Loop (HIL) refers to the process of testing a vehicle’s hardware by integrating it into a software environment and simulating different real-life scenarios for the hardware to react to. Within the product lifecycle development process, the software is typically tested before the hardware because the coding and calibration within the software must function properly. So, there are different phases where hardware and software can be tested together, but the most significant difference is that HIL testing involves simulating and testing the hardware itself. Performing HIL testing in the context of the Functional Safety standard ISO 26262—from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO)—is a method many engineers and product developers are familiar with. This methodology incorporates HIL testing within the overall product lifecycle development process. Since many different organizations perform HIL testing, along with several suppliers and companies that make hardware and software, this process can be done with various tools and equipment. Different aspects of HIL testing require responsibility from different employees, and each is essential in guaranteeing a safe and efficient product development process. As vehicle design, software, and technology grow in complexity, the process of HIL testing can mitigate harm to these systems by testing them in a controlled environment. HIL testing provides a way for organizations to verify the designs and requirements made during the early stages of the product lifecycle development process to comply with the standard. If organizations did manual testing instead of HIL testing, or its software-focused counterpart, then the hardware and software integrated into vehicles could be more tedious to verify and validate based on previously established testing requirements. HIL testing won’t uncover *every* issue, but engineers can run hardware through simulations repeatedly to ensure they are compliant with the requirements. By utilizing processes like HIL testing, engineers can test components’ functionality in simulated environments and address any identified issues.

results.title: How does hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing work? - Engineering.com
results.content: HIL testing simulates real-world conditions in a virtual environment to test complex components before physical products are made. HIL testing helps validate complex electronics by simulating the products in real-world conditions. Instead of physically testing finished prototypes, manufacturing and engineering teams can simulate actual conditions and perform testing on digital models of products, saving time and expenses. To handle testing complexities, manufacturers often turn to hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing, which simulates real-world conditions for assembled products or components. HIL testing typically connects real controller hardware with a simulated system via a combination of analog and digital I/O connections. Specific HIL testing processes vary by industry and application, but in general, the process starts with creating a digital model that simulates the physical system. By connecting real controller hardware to a simulated system, HIL testing offers more realistic testing than software-only simulation. Significant planning and development are required to build a simulation model, prepare the hardware controller for connection to the HIL system and monitor the testing.
